title: The Story of Humanity — Master Index
description: A master index linking every tradition in the corpus through 7 Universal Story Threads, 5 Meta-Narratives, and 4 Comparative Frameworks. Enables cross-tradition queries like 'How do different traditions explain creation?' or 'Compare the hero journey across civilizations.'

universal_threads.name: Creation — How the Cosmos Began
universal_threads.description: Every civilization asks: where did everything come from? The answers reveal what each culture values most — order from chaos, sacrifice, word, thought, or emergence.

key_concepts: Apsu and Tiamat as primordial waters
Izanagi and Izanami stir the sea
Heart of Sky speaks world into being
World egg cracks into sky and earth

sample_queries: How do different traditions explain the origin of the cosmos?
Compare creation from chaos vs creation from nothing across traditions
What role does sacrifice play in creation myths?

universal_threads.name: The Flood — Universal Deluge
universal_threads.description: Nearly every ancient civilization preserves a story of a catastrophic flood that destroyed the old world and enabled renewal. The flood is both destruction and baptism — an end that is also a beginning.

key_concepts: Manu warned by Matsya (fish avatar of Vishnu)
Deucalion and Pyrrha survive Zeus's flood
Yu the Great controls the flood
Failed wooden people destroyed by flood

sample_queries: Compare flood narratives across Mesopotamian, Vedic, and Biblical traditions
What common motifs appear in flood stories worldwide?
How does the Chinese flood narrative differ from the Western pattern?

universal_threads.name: The Hero's Journey — The Monomyth
universal_threads.description: Joseph Campbell's monomyth finds expression in every culture: a hero leaves the ordinary world, faces trials, achieves transformation, and returns with a boon for humanity.

key_concepts: Rama's exile and rescue of Sita
Achilles choosing glory over long life
Sundiata overcomes disability to unite Mali

sample_queries: Compare the hero's journey in Indian vs Greek vs Mesopotamian traditions
How do heroes face death across different mythologies?
What role does the companion/sidekick play in world epics?

universal_threads.name: Cosmic Cycles — Time and Eternity
universal_threads.description: Is time linear or cyclical? Most ancient traditions envision cosmic cycles of creation and destruction, with humanity currently in a declining age.

key_concepts: Five Ages: Gold, Silver, Bronze, Heroic, Iron

texts: Aztec Stone of the Five Suns

sample_queries: Compare cyclical time in Hindu, Norse, and Mesoamerican traditions
What do different traditions say about the current age of humanity?
How do traditions envision the end and renewal of the world?

universal_threads.name: The Immortality Quest — Conquering Death
universal_threads.description: From Gilgamesh seeking the herb of life to the churning of the ocean for Amrita, humanity's oldest obsession is defeating death.

key_concepts: Plant of youth lost to serpent
Nachiketas learns secret of death from Yama
Justified before Osiris for eternal afterlife

sample_queries: How do different traditions approach the quest for immortality?
Compare Gilgamesh's failure with the Vedic Amrita churning
What wisdom about death appears across world traditions?

universal_threads.name: Knowledge Theft / Divine Gift — The Fire Bringer
universal_threads.description: In many traditions, civilization-enabling knowledge is stolen from the gods or given at great cost. Fire, writing, agriculture, and wisdom all have mythic origins.

key_concepts: Odin sacrifices himself on Yggdrasil for 9 days
Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil

sample_queries: Compare Prometheus, Matarisvan, and Odin as knowledge bringers
Is knowledge a gift or a theft in different mythologies?
How do traditions view the cost of gaining wisdom?

universal_threads.name: The Underworld Descent — Journey to the Land of the Dead
universal_threads.description: The katabasis — descent to the underworld — appears in nearly every tradition. The hero goes down to death and returns transformed, bringing wisdom back to the living.

key_concepts: Must find a substitute to return
Savitri argues her husband back from death
Izanagi descends to Yomi to retrieve Izanami
Hermod rides to Hel to retrieve Baldr

sample_queries: Compare underworld descents across mythologies
What do heroes learn from visiting the land of the dead?
How do Inanna, Orpheus, and Nachiketas differ in their underworld encounters?

meta_narratives.name: Origin — Cosmogony and Anthropogony
meta_narratives.description: How each tradition explains the creation of the cosmos, the gods, and humanity. Includes divine hierarchy and the relationship between creator and creation.

meta_narratives.name: Order — Law, Dharma, and Cosmic Structure
meta_narratives.description: How each tradition structures society and aligns human behavior with cosmic law. Dharma, Ma'at, Ren, Nomos, Torah — different names for the same insight that the cosmos has a moral structure.

meta_narratives.name: Crisis — Flood, Fall, and Cosmic War
meta_narratives.description: Every tradition records a moment when the cosmic order was threatened or broken. The flood, the fall from paradise, the war of gods — these crises define the human condition.

meta_narratives.name: Quest — Hero Journey and Philosophical Seeking
meta_narratives.description: The human response to crisis: the hero ventures forth, the philosopher seeks truth, the mystic ascends. This meta-narrative encompasses both external adventure and internal transformation.

meta_narratives.name: Renewal — Eschatology and the Return of the Golden Age
meta_narratives.description: After destruction comes renewal. Every tradition envisions a return to paradise — whether through cosmic cycles, divine intervention, or human liberation (moksha, nirvana, salvation).

comparative_frameworks.name: Dumézil's Trifunctionality
comparative_frameworks.description: Georges Dumézil's theory that Indo-European societies shared a tripartite ideology: priestly/sovereign, warrior, and producer functions. Traces this across Vedic varnas, Roman flamines, Norse gods (Odin/Thor/Freyr), Celtic druids/warriors/commoners.

comparative_frameworks.name: Axial Age Mapping (800-200 BCE)
comparative_frameworks.description: Karl Jaspers' observation that philosophy and ethical religion emerged simultaneously across disconnected civilizations. Maps the parallel emergence of Buddha, Confucius, Lao Tzu, Pythagoras, Hebrew prophets, Mahavira, and Zarathustra.

comparative_frameworks.name: Knowledge Transfer Routes
comparative_frameworks.description: Historical pathways of intellectual exchange: Silk Road, Alexandria, Baghdad's House of Wisdom, Nalanda, Taxila. Tracks how ideas moved between civilizations — sometimes with clear evidence, sometimes through parallel independent development.

comparative_frameworks.name: Parallel Independent Inventions
comparative_frameworks.description: Similar ideas arising without contact — suggesting something universal about human cognition. Atomic theory (Democritus/Vaisheshika), zero (Maya/India), flood narratives, hero journeys, creation-from-sacrifice myths.

collections.sanskrit_texts: Existing Indic/Sanskrit corpus (Vedas, Upanishads, Epics, Darshana, Puranas, etc.)
collections.world_texts: New cross-cultural corpus (Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Norse, China, Japan, Africa, etc.)
collections.science_papers: Modern scientific papers bridging ancient and modern knowledge
